description: Real-Time Optimal Solar Panel Tilt and Location Calculator This project aims to maximize solar energy harvesting by developing a smart system that identifies the best geographical locations for solar panel installations. By utilizing real-time data and taking the exact latitude of the selected area into account, the system dynamically calculates the optimal tilt angle. This ensures that solar panels are positioned precisely to receive maximum solar irradiance throughout changing seasons
summary:
We developed Kardashev Ascent, a space mission design game built in Unity on real science. Players design and run a robotic surface mission. They choose a real exoplanet from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, pick a landing site, design a power system of solar panels, batteries and a radioisotope generator, and direct robots that survey, build and mine.
The game addresses the challenge by turning mission planning into decisions with consequences. Each world’s star, orbit, latitude, terrain and clouds change how much power players can produce, so poor choices cause brownouts at night and put the mission at risk. NASA POWER climatology supplies the effect of clouds. Our solar model was checked against pvlib, a standard solar-modelling library, and 793 automated tests pass. Every value is labelled as measured, derived or assumed.
This matters because real missions depend on these trade-offs, yet learners usually meet them as separate facts. Kardashev Ascent teaches systems thinking, critical reading of data and hands-on STEM. It also shows how energy decisions move a civilization up the Kardashev scale, which measures a civilization’s energy use.
details:
What it does and how it works

Kardashev Ascent is a space mission design game in which players design and run a robotic surface mission on a real exoplanet. The mission has four phases:

  1. Target selection. Players choose a world from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, such as Proxima Centauri b, TRAPPIST-1 e or Kepler-452 b. Each planet is defined by measured values: the star’s luminosity and temperature, the planet’s orbital distance, period and eccentricity, the light it receives, and its radius and mass.
  2. Landing site selection. Latitude, terrain, day length and cloud conditions decide how much sunlight a location receives.
  3. Power system design. Players place solar panels, battery storage and the lander’s RTG (radioisotope thermoelectric generator). Before building, a preview shows annual energy, capacity factor, EROI (energy return on investment) and payback time.
  4. Surface operations. Robots survey hidden deposits, build, mine, do maintenance, recharge and staff workshops. If there is too little storage at night, brownouts slow the colony’s growth. With stable power, the colony advances along the Kardashev scale, which measures a civilization’s energy use.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Systems thinking: energy, storage, robot labour and resources work as one connected system.
  • Data literacy: every value is labelled NASA, derived or assumed, so players learn to question uncertainty rather than trust every number equally.
  • Hands-on STEM learning: players learn about solar geometry, panel angles, orbital conditions and power balance by making decisions.

We want students and the public to understand that every space mission and every civilization depends on energy decisions made under physical constraints. We also want to show what honest science communication looks like.

Tools and technologies

  • Game engine: Unity 6 (6.0.6.8f1), with C# for the simulation and the user interface, built with Unity UI Toolkit.
  • Data: Python pipelines that retrieve and convert data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive (pscomppars table) and NASA POWER monthly solar climatology for 2001–2025, covering 136 locations on Earth.
  • Validation: a solar model first written in Python and checked against pvlib for sun position, air mass, angle of incidence, irradiance, cell temperature and DC power, then ported to C#.
  • Collaboration: Git, Git LFS, GitHub pull requests and Unity Smart Merge.

Creativity

  • We combine the Kardashev scale, a speculative idea about how civilizations grow, with measured NASA data and solar physics we have checked.
  • The data labelling is part of the gameplay: unknown properties are never quietly invented.
  • Players learn by discovery, since robots must survey before resources are known.
  • We use Earth’s real cloud climatology to model a fictional Earth-like planet, Viridia.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy: the physics is checked against pvlib, and the simulation is separated from the display code so it can be tested on its own.
  • Honesty: we clearly separate measured data from assumptions and game rules.
  • Scope: we focused on a strong core of solar power, storage, robots and operations. Launch and trajectory planning, multiple planets, climate simulation and advanced energy sources are left as future work.
  • Known limitations: some exoplanet properties, such as axial tilt and atmosphere, are unknown. The panel preview does not yet support tidally locked planets.
  • Accessibility: complex science is shown through visual feedback that players can act on.
